transcript:
This message comes from the UPS Store.
Open this holiday to help with all your small business needs.
Find a store near you at theupsstore.com.
Most locations are independently owned.
Products, services, pricing, and hours of operation may vary.
See Center for details.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Republicans are weighing their next steps following the loss of both chambers of Congress.
The president of the Conservative Heritage Foundation says the party needs to confront the economic fallout from the war in Iran.
Kevin Roberts helped shape Project 2025, the policy blueprint behind many of the Trump administration's priorities.
Roberts says heritage had expected stronger economic growth before the conflict began.
The week before the war in Iran, in fact, our chief economist at Heritage, Dr. E.J. Antony, has predicted that there would have been a Trump economic boom had he not started the war in Iran.
The point is that Iran, especially by increasing energy prices, aggravated those inflationary pressures.
That prediction reflects the Heritage Foundation's assessment of what might have happened without the war.
Democrats will take control of the House and Senate in January.
The Trump administration says it's planning to intervene in a Texas lawsuit against Planned Parenthood.
NPR's Shonda Lee Stuster reports the case centers on allegations that the organization improperly collected Medicaid payments.
In what is regarded as an attempt to shut down Planned Parenthood, attorneys for the Justice Department filed a notice of appearance to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas.
The notice follows days after Republicans, including Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lost their seats to Democrats.
Paxton has been handling the years-long legal battle against Planned Parenthood.
The lawsuit accuses Planned Parenthood of Medicaid fraud, and the state is seeking to recover $1.8 billion.
Susan Baker Manning, general counsel for Planned Parenthood, said in a statement that the organization is going to "fight this every step of the way, including at trial."
NPR has reached out to the Justice Department for comment on the lawsuit, but has not received a response.
Shonda Lee Stuster, NPR News.
Worshipers gathered for a mass as Pope Leo wraps up his three-day visit to Uruguay.
NPR's Kerry Kahn reports the pontiff says Catholics have a role in public life and the church and government can work together for the common good.
Pope Leo hasn't shied away from taking on Uruguay's tightly enforced division between church and state.
In a poor community outside the capital Montevideo, Leo urged more cooperation between the church, civil society and the government to help the poor.
We must awaken from our inertia and advocate together for the common good.
Speaking to his largest gathering in Montevideo's historic football stadium, Leo said the government does have a role, but nothing compares to God's love.
Kerry Kahn, NPR News, Montevideo.
This is NPR News in Washington.
This year's El Nino could be the strongest on record. The natural climate pattern affects weather across the globe.
NPR's Ava Berger reports that some parts of the U.S. are feeling the impact and it's driving an El Nino economy.
Drainage contractors are very popular in California right now.
Jim Garner, who owns a construction company, says he's booked four months in advance.
In fact, it's to the point where I can barely keep up with it.
California has already seen some of El Nino's impacts, higher sea level, greater chance for coastal flooding.
But it's not just California that will see different weather this year.
Across the country, warmer and wetter conditions are forecasted for most of the continental U.S.
So a range of companies are either preparing to or are already seeing a bump in business.
We're talking tire cellars, ski mountains, and mold sniffing dogs.
That's not a group that typically has something in common.
Thanks to El Nino, now they do.
Ava Berger and Pierre News.
At least 22 people were injured when a strong earthquake shook central Japan early this morning.
The magnitude 5.7 quake shattered store windows and sent books tumbling from shelves.
Some people were hurt while trying to flee buildings.
Transit officials say bullet trains are running at reduced speeds as a precaution.
Authorities are warning residents to prepare for strong aftershocks in the coming days.
I'm Windsor Johnston, and you're listening to NPR News from Washington.

Trump administration plans to intervene in Texas Medicaid fraud lawsuit against Planned Parenthood, seeking $1.8 billion
Pope Leo wraps up three-day visit to Uruguay with mass at Montevideo football stadium, urging church-state cooperation for common good
Strong El Nino expected this year, driving business boom for drainage contractors, ski mountains and tire dealers
Magnitude 5.7 earthquake strikes central Japan, injuring at least 22 people and slowing bullet trains
